Well, let's forget about MGTOW for just a second and consider this statement on its own. Is this a maxim (an expression of a general truth or principle), that it's a bad idea to fight human nature?

What is human nature? I would say that it's the collection of instinctive traits and behaviors common to our species. Human nature is what we've evolved to do. I can make two arguments that fighting human nature may be in your best interests.

First, evolution doesn't serve the individual; it serves the species. This is the observation Dawkins makes in The Selfish Gene. Evolution (and therefore the instincts it creates) is perfectly happy to sacrifice you, as an individual, sometimes brutally in order to help the species. Therefore, if your goal is individual happiness, then your goal may be at odds with evolution.

Second argument: our environment has changed rapidly over the last 10,000 years. As a result, we may still have some instincts that served our ancestors well, but work against us. A good example is that you have an instinct to crave salt. For your ancestors, salt was hard to get. The craving motivated them to expend the effort. But for us, salt is easy to get. As a result, blindly following the craving actually makes us sick.

So there are two arguments saying that it is not a maxim that fighting human nature is a bad thing. In fact, if you want to be happy and healthy, there may be times when you need to fight your nature.

Buddha is right. " this was hobo or bum music." These were shared around campfires in hobo jungles next to the railroad tracks late at night. It is a folk song about a hobo's idea of paradise, a modern version of the medieval concept of Cockaigne. It is a place where "hens lay soft boiled eggs" and there are "cigarette trees." McClintock, also known by his "hobo" name of Haywire Mac, claimed to have written the song in 1895, based on tales from his youth hoboing through the United States, but some believe that at least aspects of the song have existed for far longer. In fact, some think it may have aspects of "An Invitation to Lubberland", which was a broadside ballad first printed in 1685.

Before recording the song, McClintock cleaned it up considerably from the version he sang as a street busker in the 1890s. Originally the song described a child being recruited into hobo life by tales of the "big rock candy mountain". In later years, when McClintock appeared in court as part of a copyright dispute, he cited the original words of the song, the last stanza of which was:

The punk rolled up his big blue eyes
And said to the jocker, "Sandy,
I've hiked and hiked and wandered too,
But I ain't seen any candy.
I've hiked and hiked till my feet are sore
